title: Layer 5 Pyramidal Cells
intro: Layer 5 holds the cortex's largest pyramidal cells and its main output. Thick-tufted cells send the cortex's commands to the brainstem, spinal cord and thalamus; slender-tufted cells talk to other cortex and the striatum. Thick-tufted layer 5 cells are also the best-studied neurons in computational neuroscience, because their long apical dendrite turns them into two coupled integration zones whose coincidence produces bursts.

items: Thick-tufted (TTPC; pyramidal-tract or extratelencephalic, PT/ET): large somata in layer 5b, an apical trunk about 1 mm long in rodents ending in a big tuft in layer 1, intrinsically bursting or doublet firing, a strong h-current that makes the tuft and soma fire at different phases. Axons go to the brainstem, spinal cord (in motor cortex), superior colliculus, pons and higher-order thalamus, with branches to the striatum. They are the 'driver' input to higher-order thalamic nuclei (Sherman & Guillery 2006).

Slender-tufted or thin-tufted (STPC; intratelencephalic, IT): smaller cells, often in layer 5a, with thinner apical dendrites and small tufts, regular spiking. Axons go to other cortical areas on both sides and to the striatum.

The two classes connect asymmetrically: IT cells excite PT cells, but PT cells rarely excite IT cells (Morishima & Kawaguchi 2006; Brown & Hestrin 2009). Information flows from the cortico-cortical network into the output cells, not back.

blocks.text: Dendrites: three zones and BAC firing

A thick-tufted cell has a fast spike initiation zone at the axon near the soma, NMDA spike zones in its thin basal and tuft branches, and a calcium spike initiation zone near the main bifurcation of the apical trunk, about 500 to 800 µm from the soma in rat. Distal tuft input alone is attenuated so much that it barely moves the soma. Larkum, Zhu and Sakmann (1999) showed what happens when the two arrive together: a somatic action potential back-propagates up the trunk, and if it coincides (within roughly 20 to 30 ms) with tuft input, the combination triggers a calcium spike in the trunk that flows back to the soma as a long depolarisation and produces a burst of two to four spikes. This is back-propagation-activated calcium spike firing, BAC firing. A single spike therefore means 'feedforward input', and a burst means 'feedforward input that matched feedback'.

Larkum (2013) proposed that this is a general cellular mechanism for associating the cortex's two streams: bottom-up input from layer 4 and thalamus on the basal dendrites, and top-down, contextual input from higher areas and higher-order thalamus on the tuft. Suzuki and Larkum (2020) showed that anaesthetics decouple the two zones, linking this mechanism to conscious perception. Naud and Sprekeler (2018) and Payeur et al. (2021) built on it: bursts versus single spikes could multiplex two signals in one spike train, and burst-dependent plasticity could carry learning signals for credit assignment.

items: Mainen and Sejnowski (1996): the classic demonstration that the same channels placed in different morphologies (stellate, L2/3 pyramidal, thick-tufted L5) produce regular spiking, bursting or chattering. Dendritic shape alone changes firing class.

Hay, Hill, Schurmann, Segev and Markram (2011): the reference detailed model of a rat thick-tufted L5 cell. A reconstructed morphology with about 200 compartments and ten channel types (Na transient and persistent, several K, Ca high- and low-voltage-activated, SK, Ih), fitted by multi-objective optimisation to reproduce both somatic firing and BAC firing. Available on ModelDB (accession 139653) and widely reused.

Reduced models of BAC firing: two-compartment models with a somatic and an apical calcium compartment (Larkum et al. 2004; Naud et al. 2014, who fitted a two-compartment adaptive integrate-and-fire model to L5 recordings and reproduced bursting from coincidences); Bahl et al. (2012) reduced the cell to a few compartments while keeping the dendritic calcium zone.

Machine-learning abstractions: Beniaguev, Segev and London (2021) trained a temporal convolutional network to mimic the Hay L5 model and needed a deep network of five to eight layers, a measure of how much computation one such neuron does. With NMDA receptors removed a single hidden layer sufficed.

Point neurons: Izhikevich intrinsically bursting preset (c = −55, d = 4); AdEx with a high reset (Naud et al. 2008 bursting parameters). These capture the firing class but not the coincidence detection between zones.
Network models: Blue Brain's L5_TTPC1, TTPC2, UTPC and STPC m-types; layer 5 populations in Potjans-Diesmann (about 4,850 E cells) and in the Allen V1 model.

blocks.text: Try it: soma and dendrite as two compartments

The widget runs a minimal two-compartment integrate-and-fire neuron: current is injected into the dendrite and spreads to the soma through a coupling conductance. At the default setting the soma fires a regular train. Lower the coupling below about 0.2 and the dendrite still charges up but the soma barely notices, just as tuft input alone hardly drives a thick-tufted cell. Raise the coupling and the same dendritic input drives faster somatic firing. A full BAC model adds a regenerative calcium spike in the dendritic compartment, which this simplified version leaves out.
What this means for your SNN

items: If your column has an output layer that should signal 'prediction confirmed' or 'context matches', give layer 5 cells two compartments and make the apical compartment burst-triggering. Read bursts and single spikes as separate signals.
Route top-down and contextual input to the apical compartment, bottom-up input to the basal/somatic one, and put SST-like inhibition on the apical compartment so it can be gated.
Wire IT → PT but not PT → IT, and send PT output out of the column (to a model thalamus or motor stage).
Use the Hay et al. model as a ground truth when you test a reduced model: compare burst probability as a function of the timing between somatic and tuft input.
